questions.stem: Six months into a £4.6 million coastal path resurfacing scheme, the finance ledger shows £1.42 million spent against a plan of £1.61 million. Your quantity surveyor confirms the work in the ground matches the plan, and that two contractors have not yet submitted applications covering roughly £190,000 of completed work. The regeneration sponsor has seen the ledger figure and has already written to the team congratulating them on the underspend. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Report cost incurred including an accrual for the completed but uninvoiced work, and correct the sponsor's reading of the position straight away.
options.rationale: Cost control works on what the project has consumed, not on what has been paid for. Correcting a favourable misreading immediately also protects the sponsor from committing the phantom saving somewhere else.

options.text: Report the ledger figure as the position and note the outstanding applications in a footnote.
options.rationale: This treats the accounting system's cash view as the project's cost position, then buries the correction where a reader will skim past it. The headline number is the one people act on.

options.text: Wait for the applications to arrive next month and report a single corrected figure then.
options.rationale: Delaying a known correction to keep one clean report means the sponsor spends a month making decisions against a number you already know to be wrong.

options.text: Press both contractors to submit their applications before the report is issued so the ledger catches up.
options.rationale: It fixes this month's paperwork rather than the reporting basis, so the position goes wrong again the next time a supplier is slow. Chasing an artefact is not the same as reporting the truth.

questions.explanation: The date money leaves the bank has nothing to do with the date the project consumed it, and cost control depends on the second. Any reporting basis that lets uninvoiced work sit outside the position will drift favourable during delivery and snap adverse near the end, which is the worst possible pattern for a sponsor who is deciding whether to act. A favourable variance carries the same duty of investigation as an adverse one.
questions.mindset: Report what the project has consumed, not what the ledger has processed.

questions.stem: Your squad builds monitoring software for an aquaculture operator and is funded at £310,000 a quarter. Since adding a high-frequency sensor feed four sprints ago, the telemetry and storage charges the product carries have risen about nine per cent each sprint and now run to £11,000 a month. The engineers argue this is infrastructure and belongs on the platform team's budget rather than the squad's. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Bring the run-cost trend into the squad's cost forecast and put the resulting trade-off to the product owner.
options.rationale: The charge is a consequence of the squad's own design choices, so showing it inside their envelope is what lets the sampling rate be weighed against the features it displaces.

options.text: Agree with the engineers and ask the platform team to absorb the charge on their budget.
options.rationale: Moving a cost to another ledger does not reduce it, and it severs the feedback between a design decision and its price — after which nothing restrains the next increase.

options.text: Reduce the sensor sampling frequency now to stop the growth before the quarter closes.
options.rationale: It acts on the cost without anyone weighing what the feed is worth. A product decision taken as a finance reflex is still a product decision, and it has been taken by the wrong person.

options.text: Raise a funding request for the increase to be added to this quarter's envelope.
options.rationale: Asking for more money before establishing whether the spend earns its keep makes funding growth the default answer to any rising line, and the underlying trend goes unexamined.

questions.explanation: Operating cost that a team's own choices generate belongs in that team's cost picture, because visibility is what converts an invisible drift into a decision someone can take. Pushing it to a shared budget is not a saving; it removes the only signal that would ever prompt a design change. Where a running cost is rising on a curve, the forecast should carry the curve, not the current month.
questions.mindset: Put a cost where the decisions that cause it are taken.

questions.stem: A hospital pharmacy automation programme holds a contingency reserve of £480,000. The works are about forty per cent complete by cost and £330,000 of that reserve has already been drawn, mostly for ceiling voids and asbestos found during strip-out. The risk register shows the heavier exposure still ahead: integration with the dispensing robots and a commissioning window that cannot move. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Re-price the risks that remain open and compare that exposure with the contingency still available.
options.rationale: Contingency is only adequate or inadequate relative to what is left to happen. Comparing the two turns an uncomfortable percentage into a number the sponsor can act on.

options.text: Take the resulting shortfall to the sponsor now, with options for closing it.
options.rationale: A funding gap identified with sixty per cent of the work still to run has options attached; the same gap found at commissioning has none. Early notice is the whole value of the analysis.

options.text: Suspend all further contingency drawdown until the percentage complete catches up with the percentage of reserve consumed.
options.rationale: This rations by arithmetic rather than by exposure. Refusing a legitimate drawdown does not make the risk go away — it just relocates the overspend to a later report.

options.text: Transfer funds from the management reserve to top the contingency back up.
options.rationale: The management reserve is not the project manager's to move, and using it here reclassifies a well-understood shortfall as an unforeseen event, which is exactly the confusion the two reserves exist to prevent.

options.text: Re-baseline the cost plan so the drawn contingency is absorbed into the baseline and the variance disappears.
options.rationale: Redrawing the line to match the position removes the trend that is the actual warning. Re-baselining is a response to an authorised change of plan, not a way of tidying a bad signal.

questions.explanation: Reserve adequacy is a forward-looking question, so the meaningful comparison is between remaining exposure and remaining cover, never between consumption and progress. Drawdown running ahead of completion is a prompt to re-price, not a verdict in itself: it can be entirely rational if the front of the programme carried the risk. What makes a reserve position reportable is the gap it implies at the end, and that gap is worth most to a sponsor while there is still time to fund or avoid it.
questions.mindset: Judge a reserve by what is still to come, not by how much of it has gone.

questions.stem: The relining of a kiln at a ceramics works was estimated at 480 labour hours at £65 an hour. The job is finished. The contractor supplied a less experienced crew charged at £58 an hour, and the crew took 540 hours. Your finance business partner sees a total cost variance of only £120 against the estimate and proposes closing the item without comment. Separate the variance into its two parts before you agree with her.

blanks.label: Rate variance, in £ (state the amount only)
blanks.rationale: The rate variance is the difference in hourly rate applied to the hours actually worked: (65 − 58) × 540 = £3,780 favourable. Cheaper labour saved this much, whatever else happened.

blanks.label: Usage variance, in £ (state the amount only)
blanks.rationale: The usage variance is the extra hours priced at the estimated rate: (540 − 480) × 65 = £3,900 adverse. The crew took sixty hours longer than the job was planned to need.

blanks.label: Which of the two parts is adverse
blanks.rationale: The usage part is adverse by £3,900 and the rate part is favourable by £3,780, which is why they net to £120 adverse. The netted figure conceals two effects roughly thirty times its own size.

questions.explanation: A small net variance is not evidence that nothing happened; it is often evidence that two large effects have cancelled. Decomposition matters because the parts behave differently in future: a rate advantage may hold for the rest of the contract while an hours overrun may signal that every similar package is under-estimated. The question worth asking of any variance is not how big it is but whether its causes will repeat.
questions.mindset: A netted figure hides its causes, so decompose before concluding there is nothing to explain.

questions.stem: Your forecast for a water treatment upgrade shows completion £310,000 above the £5.2 million cost baseline, driven by ground conditions that were mis-assumed at design. The project also holds £400,000 of contingency for identified risks, none of which have yet occurred. Your sponsor, who briefs the board on Thursday, suggests applying £310,000 of the contingency so the report shows no variance, on the grounds that the money sits inside the project's total budget either way. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Report the overrun as a baseline variance and hold the contingency against the risks it was sized for, bringing drawdown requests only as those risks occur.
options.rationale: It keeps the two numbers answering the two different questions they were built to answer: how far the plan has moved, and how much cover remains for what has not yet happened.

options.text: Apply the contingency as suggested, since the money is inside the authorised project budget in either case.
options.rationale: Being inside the total budget is confused here with being available. The cover for every identified risk would be spent on an event that is not a risk at all, leaving the project exposed and the board unaware.

options.text: Decline and escalate immediately to the board's finance director without going back to the sponsor.
options.rationale: It skips the conversation in which a sponsor under pressure can be shown why the proposal misfires, and spends significant credibility on a disagreement nobody has yet tried to resolve.

options.text: Apply the contingency but disclose the drawdown in the notes to the report.
options.rationale: A disclosed misuse is still a misuse, and boards read headlines. This buys the appearance of transparency while producing exactly the decision the sponsor asked for.

questions.explanation: Contingency is priced cover for specific identified risks, so spending it on a realised estimating error is not an accounting choice but a reduction in the project's protection that no one has agreed to. The general rule is that a baseline overrun and a reserve drawdown are different events with different authorisers, and collapsing one into the other destroys the information both were built to carry. Where a sponsor proposes it, the useful response is to show what cover would be left rather than to argue about propriety.
questions.mindset: Money set aside for what might happen is not available for what already has.

questions.stem: A national parks authority has asked you to advise its estates team, which needs three different cost figures over the coming year and has been producing all of them the same way. Each situation below differs in what information exists and what the number will be used for. Match each situation to the estimating approach that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The board wants an order-of-magnitude figure within two days, to decide whether refurbishing a visitor centre is worth exploring at all. A comparable centre was refurbished last year.
Fifty-eight kilometres of footpath must be resurfaced to a standard specification, and the authority holds ten years of reliable cost-per-kilometre records for that exact work.
Detailed design for a bridge replacement is complete, and the figure produced will become the sum the authority is contractually held to.

options.text: Analogous estimating from the comparable scheme
options.rationale: A gate decision about whether to explore an idea needs a figure of the right order within days, and a genuinely similar recent scheme supplies that. Accuracy beyond the decision's needs would be wasted effort.

options.text: Parametric estimating from the historic cost per kilometre
options.rationale: A repeated unit of work, a stable specification and a reliable rate history are the exact conditions under which a per-unit model outperforms building the estimate up from scratch.

options.text: Bottom-up estimating from the designed quantities
options.rationale: A figure that becomes a contractual commitment has to be defensible line by line, and only aggregating the priced components gives you something you can hold a dispute against.

options.text: Three-point estimating across optimistic, likely and pessimistic cases
options.rationale: Not used. Three-point work expresses the uncertainty around a base estimate that already exists; it refines a figure rather than producing one, so it is a companion to any of the three above rather than an alternative to them.

questions.explanation: The right estimating approach follows two things: what information you actually have, and what decision the number has to support. Effort spent building precision that the decision cannot use is waste, and precision claimed without the data to support it is worse than a stated range. The recurring failure is an organisation that has one method and applies it everywhere, producing figures that are simultaneously too slow for gate decisions and too crude for contracts.
questions.mindset: Match the estimate's precision to the decision it must carry, not to the time available.

questions.stem: Your squad builds practice software for a group of dental surgeries and works to a quarterly funding envelope. Three weeks from the quarter end, £22,000 of the envelope is unspent because a planned contractor engagement was not needed. The product owner proposes buying a two-year analytics licence with it, saying the team has wanted the tool for a while and the money will otherwise be lost. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the licence judged on its own merits against the next quarter's priorities, and report the underspend with its cause.
options.rationale: It separates two decisions that have been fused: whether the tool is worth buying, and what to do about money that is about to lapse. Only the first should determine the purchase.

options.text: Buy the licence, since the team wants it and the funding disappears at the quarter end.
options.rationale: The trigger for the purchase is the calendar rather than the need, which is how organisations acquire tools nobody has evaluated. It also teaches finance that the envelope is a target to be hit.

options.text: Split the licence into smaller purchases that sit under the approval threshold, so it can be bought quickly.
options.rationale: Structuring spend to stay under a control is a governance breach whatever the intention behind it, and it is usually obvious in the ledger afterwards.

options.text: Say nothing and let the £22,000 lapse quietly at the quarter end.
options.rationale: Silence forfeits the chance to explain why the money was not needed, so finance draws its own conclusion and sizes the next envelope on a pattern nobody has described.

questions.explanation: A funding envelope is a limit on what may be spent, not an amount that must be consumed, and treating a period boundary as a deadline to spend by inverts the purpose of having one. The transferable move is to decouple the purchase decision from the calendar and to make the underspend and its cause visible, because unexplained variances are what make the next allocation worse. Spending to protect an allocation costs real money to preserve a notional entitlement.
questions.mindset: An envelope is a ceiling, not a target.

questions.stem: An air ambulance charity's donor platform runs three plan-driven integration work packages alongside an iterative front-end team. For four consecutive weeks the three package managers have each reported ninety per cent complete, while their costs have continued to accrue at the planned rate. The front-end team, which claims value only on accepted increments, shows no such pattern. What should the project manager do about the integration packages?

options.text: Replace subjective percentage claims with an objective rule, such as claiming on completed milestones or nothing until acceptance.
options.rationale: It removes the judgement that is producing the distortion. A rule anyone can apply the same way is what makes progress figures comparable week to week.

options.text: Ask the three managers to be more realistic in their assessments in future.
options.rationale: It treats a measurement design problem as a problem of individual honesty. Optimism at ninety per cent is a well-known property of subjective claiming, not a character defect in these three people.

options.text: Accept the claims and reduce the forecast by an allowance based on your own judgement of where the packages really are.
options.rationale: Patching the output while leaving the input broken makes the forecast depend on one person's private correction factor, which nobody else can audit or reproduce.

options.text: Stop reporting percentage complete for these packages and report cost incurred only.
options.rationale: Removing the progress dimension leaves a cost figure with nothing to compare it against, and spend without progress is exactly the pairing that makes a cost report interpretable.

questions.explanation: Cost performance information is only as good as the progress measurement feeding it, and any claiming method that relies on an estimate of remaining effort will bunch near completion. The general fix is to make claiming binary or milestone-based so that the rule, not the claimant, determines the number. This is also why an iterative team that claims only on accepted work rarely shows the same distortion: acceptance is an external event rather than a self-assessment.
questions.mindset: Design the claiming rule so that progress is observed rather than asserted.

questions.stem: A coastal defence scheme is funded from a capital allocation profiled at £3.1 million this financial year and £2.4 million next, and the funder's terms do not allow movement between years. A consent delay means £600,000 of works planned for February will now fall in April, leaving this year's allocation under-consumed and next year's over-committed. The contractor offers to accelerate for an additional £145,000 to keep the works in-year. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish with the funder whether the in-year allocation is genuinely irrecoverable, then put the acceleration cost and the re-profiling option to the sponsor as a priced choice.
options.rationale: It tests the constraint everyone is assuming before spending against it, and leaves the trade-off between £145,000 and a funding profile with the person accountable for both.

options.text: Accept the acceleration offer, since losing £600,000 of allocation is plainly worse than paying £145,000.
options.rationale: It spends real money to protect an accounting boundary that nobody has confirmed is hard. Funders frequently permit carry-forward or re-profiling when asked early, and the question has not been asked.

options.text: Re-profile the works into next year and inform the funder once the revised programme is issued.
options.rationale: It treats a funding condition as an administrative detail. The funder may have commitments of its own against the allocation, and presenting the change after the fact removes any option they might have offered.

options.text: Bring forward other packages into February so the allocation is fully consumed this year.
options.rationale: Re-sequencing work to consume a budget makes the money disappear on schedule without buying anything the project needed sooner, and it disturbs a sequence that was set for delivery reasons.

questions.explanation: A funding limit is a constraint on when money may be spent, which is a different thing from how much is available, and the two are routinely confused under time pressure. The disciplined response is to test whether the constraint binds, then price the options it leaves and hand the decision to whoever owns both the money and the outcome. Paying to preserve an allocation can be entirely rational — but only once someone has compared the acceleration cost with the cost of the delay it prevents.
questions.mindset: Confirm that a constraint is real before you spend money to satisfy it.

questions.stem: An engineer on your community radio platform team mentions that for the past five months he has been paying $38 a month on his own card for a monitoring service the whole team now relies on, and asks whether he can be reimbursed. He says he did not raise it at the time because the amount was too small to bother the budget with, and two other small services are in the same position. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reimburse him through the normal route and bring all three subscriptions into the product's recorded cost base.
options.rationale: It settles the individual's out-of-pocket position and, more importantly, converts three invisible recurring costs into ones the forecast and the renewal decisions can see.

options.text: Reimburse him from petty cash and leave the arrangement as it is.
options.rationale: It solves the person's problem and none of the project's. The cost keeps recurring outside every forecast, and the team's real run rate stays understated.

options.text: Decline the claim and ask him to cancel the service, since it was never authorised.
options.rationale: It punishes initiative and withdraws a service the team depends on, without anyone weighing what the service is worth. Unauthorised is a reason to review, not automatically to stop.

options.text: Ask him to carry on paying and submit a single expense claim each quarter.
options.rationale: It leaves an individual financing an organisational cost and keeps the spend arriving as an expense claim, which is exactly the route that keeps small recurring charges out of the cost base.

questions.explanation: Small recurring costs are dangerous not because of their size but because of their invisibility: nothing that never enters the cost base is ever reviewed, renewed deliberately, or included in a run rate. The rule that transfers is that a cost should be recorded where it is consumed as soon as it is known, however small, and that the threshold for recording is much lower than the threshold for approving. Personal cards are a symptom worth reading, because they usually mean the proper route felt too slow.
questions.mindset: Anything the team depends on belongs in the cost base, however small the number.

questions.stem: You have taken over cost control on a further education college's campus rewiring programme, and the two situations below have arisen in the same reporting period. Each turns on where the money should properly come from or how it should properly appear. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A design assumption about the existing risers has proved wrong, and the remaining electrical work will cost £140,000 more than budgeted. The project manager should ensure the increase is
A framework call-off signed this week commits £300,000 of switchgear that will not be delivered or invoiced for eight months. In this month's cost report that amount should

options.text: re-estimated on the remaining work and taken through change control as a variance to the cost baseline
options.rationale: A wrong assumption is an error in the plan rather than an event that might or might not have happened, so it belongs in the baseline conversation where someone with authority decides whether to fund it or reduce scope.

options.text: appear as a commitment against the baseline even though nothing has been spent or invoiced
options.rationale: Signing removes the organisation's freedom to spend that money on anything else, which is the moment the budget is genuinely consumed. Waiting for the invoice would leave eight months of apparent headroom that does not exist.

options.text: be met from the contingency reserve on the project manager's own authority
options.rationale: Not used. Contingency covers identified risks that occur, so it fits neither an estimating error nor an ordinary purchase commitment. Drawing on it for either hides a baseline problem and quietly removes cover from the risks it was sized against.

questions.explanation: Two questions recur in cost control and are easily merged: what has changed about the plan, and what has the project already tied itself to. Baseline changes need authority because they alter what was agreed; commitments need recording because they alter what remains available even before any money moves. Reserves answer neither question, which is why they are the wrong instrument for both and the most commonly reached-for one.
questions.mindset: Ask what a number is evidence of before deciding where it belongs.

questions.stem: At a port logistics terminal, two engineers have been booking their time to the wrong charge code for six weeks. The effect is that your quay crane project appears £46,000 underspent and a neighbouring berth project appears overspent by the same amount. You built next quarter's cost forecast on your figures a fortnight ago and the sponsor has seen it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the actuals corrected at source, restate the affected reports, and re-issue the forecast that was built on them.
options.rationale: It repairs the record, the outputs derived from it, and the decisions in flight. Anything less leaves someone holding a number that has quietly stopped being true.

options.text: Adjust the forecast to compensate for the error without changing the ledger, since the total across both projects is right.
options.rationale: It creates a forecast that cannot be reconciled to the accounts and leaves two wrong records in place. Anyone auditing later finds a discrepancy with no explanation attached.

options.text: Note the cause and move on, because the errors net out across the portfolio and no money has actually been lost.
options.rationale: The organisation's total is right and every decision taken at project level is wrong, which is where the decisions are actually taken. Netting out at the top is not a control.

options.text: Ask finance to journal the correction quietly before month end so no restatement is needed.
options.rationale: Correcting without restating leaves the already-issued reports wrong for good, and the people who acted on them never learn that the basis moved.

questions.explanation: Cost actuals are an input to forecasts, variance analysis and reserve decisions, so a coding error does not stay contained in the ledger. The rule is to correct at source rather than downstream, and to restate anything already published, because a correction that leaves the original circulating produces two numbers with equal standing. Persistent mis-coding is also a signal about how time is captured, which is worth more than the individual correction.
questions.mindset: Correct the record where it broke, and tell everyone who used it.

questions.stem: A nature recovery grant funds your squad at £270,000 a quarter to build a service for farmers to submit habitat data, and the funding case rests on the number of farms submitting. Two quarters in, the squad has shipped every release it planned and submissions remain flat at about forty a month against a target of four hundred. The next funding review is in three weeks. How should the project manager prepare for it?

options.text: Take the evidence to the review as a decision, with options that include a reduced envelope and stopping, alongside what would have to be true for continuing to make sense.
options.rationale: It puts the funder in a position to decide rather than to approve, which is what a funding review is for when the outcome the money was justified on has not moved.

options.text: Request continuation and propose spending part of the next quarter on marketing the service to farmers.
options.rationale: It assumes awareness is the problem without testing the assumption, and asks for another £270,000 to investigate something two quarters of data have not yet explained.

options.text: Pause the squad now so that no further grant money is consumed before the review.
options.rationale: It pre-empts a decision that belongs to the funder and disperses a team that may still be the right one, on three weeks' impatience.

options.text: Report against releases delivered, which the squad has met in full, and note submissions as a secondary measure.
options.rationale: Changing the headline measure to one you are hitting is how funding survives a failed hypothesis, and it delays the reckoning to a point where far more money has gone.

questions.explanation: Money released in periods buys the option to stop, and that option only has value if someone is willing to exercise it. When delivery is healthy but the outcome the funding rested on has not moved, the honest framing is that the hypothesis is in question, not the team. Bringing options at different envelope sizes — including zero — is what makes a periodic review a control rather than a ritual.
questions.mindset: Incremental funding is only a control if stopping is genuinely on the table.

questions.stem: The chart plots the cumulative cost baseline for a wind-monitoring network as a rising curve, against the funding authorised for each quarter as a series of steps. The total authorised for the year exceeds the total baseline, and your finance partner has concluded from that alone that the plan is affordable. Select the point at which the plan first requires more money than has been authorised.

graphic.title: Cumulative cost baseline curve against stepped quarterly funding authorisations
graphic.caption: Select a point on the chart. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between points, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Late in quarter two, where the curve rises steeply but stays below the step
regions.rationale: The curve is climbing fast here, but it is still under the authorised line. A steep gradient is a statement about spend rate, not about whether the money has been made available.

regions.label: Early in quarter three, where the curve crosses above the step
regions.rationale: This is the first moment at which cumulative requirement exceeds cumulative authorisation, so it is the point at which the project would need funding it has not been granted. Everything before it is affordable; everything after it depends on this being resolved.

regions.label: The steepest section of the curve, in quarter four
regions.rationale: The most expensive period is not necessarily the unaffordable one. Steepness is a rate of spend, and reading it as the problem is the most common misreading of a funding chart.

regions.label: The final point, where the curve meets the total for the year
regions.rationale: At the end the totals reconcile, which is precisely why the year-end comparison your finance partner made is misleading. A plan can be affordable in total and unfundable in the middle.

questions.explanation: A funding limit constrains the profile of spend, not only its total, so affordability has to be tested period by period against the cumulative authorisation. The breach is the first crossing point, and the response is to re-profile the work, seek a revised authorisation, or accept a delay — decided while there is still time to choose. Comparing annual totals is the standard error, because it answers a question about size when the constraint is about timing.
questions.mindset: Test a plan against the money available when it is needed, not against the money available in total.

questions.stem: A supplier fitting out a textile recycling plant offers two per cent off a £480,000 invoice if it is paid within ten days rather than the contractual sixty. The saving would be about £9,600. Your project budget is unaffected by when the invoice is paid, but the organisation runs a working capital facility and the treasury team manages payment timing across all suppliers. Your project accountant says it is your call. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Put the offer and the numbers to treasury as an organisational decision, with a recommendation and a deadline.
options.rationale: The saving is real but the cash it consumes belongs to the organisation, so the decision needs the person who can see what else that cash is doing over the same ten days.

options.text: Instruct accounts payable to pay early and record the £9,600 as a project saving.
options.rationale: It commits the organisation's cash on the project's authority. A saving in your column can be more than offset by borrowing costs in a column you cannot see.

options.text: Decline the offer, since the project's budget position is identical either way.
options.rationale: It discards a genuine saving because it does not appear in the reporting line the project manager is measured on, which is optimising the report rather than the outcome.

options.text: Ask the supplier to convert the discount into reduced rates on future invoices instead.
options.rationale: It trades a specific, decided saving for a vaguer future one, and still leaves the question of who owns the cash timing unasked.

questions.explanation: Project cost control sits inside an organisation's finances, and decisions that are neutral to a project budget are frequently not neutral to the organisation. The transferable habit is to identify whose resource a decision actually consumes and to route it there with the numbers already worked out, rather than either seizing the decision or dropping it. Being told it is your call is not the same as it being yours to make.
questions.mindset: Work out whose money a decision really spends before deciding it.

questions.stem: Your squad builds a translation service for a legal publisher and works to a €180,000 quarterly envelope. Six weeks in, the machine translation vendor raises its per-character price with thirty days' notice, adding about €14,000 to this quarter and more thereafter. The product owner's first reaction is to find the money somewhere quietly. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Quantify the increase against the envelope and identify precisely what work it would displace.
options.rationale: An unfunded cost is only a decision once someone can see what it costs in delivered work. The displacement is the part that makes the trade-off real rather than notional.

options.text: Put the choice — absorb it, displace work, or seek additional funding — to whoever holds the envelope.
options.rationale: The envelope holder is the only person who can legitimately decide between less scope and more money, and presenting all three options prevents the decision defaulting to the least visible one.

options.text: Absorb it by cutting the team's training and conference allowance for the quarter.
options.rationale: It takes the reduction from the least visible line rather than the least valuable one, which is how teams end up funding vendor increases out of their own development over several quarters.

options.text: Migrate to a cheaper vendor within the current sprint to avoid the increase entirely.
options.rationale: A technical migration chosen on price under a thirty-day clock imports quality, integration and exit risks that nobody has had time to assess.

options.text: Ask the vendor to honour the old pricing and plan on the assumption that they will.
options.rationale: Asking is reasonable; planning on the answer is not. A forecast that depends on someone else's goodwill is not a forecast, and the request costs nothing only if you also plan for a refusal.

questions.explanation: A fixed funding envelope converts every cost increase into a scope conversation, and the useful discipline is to make that conversation explicit rather than to absorb the increase invisibly. Quantifying the displacement first is what allows the decision to be taken on value rather than on which budget line is easiest to raid. Where a cost rise is structural rather than one-off, the same analysis should be carried into the next period's request instead of being re-fought each quarter.
questions.mindset: Inside a fixed envelope, every extra cost is a decision about what will not be built.

questions.stem: A rural broadband programme's board has approved adding twelve street cabinets to reach three outlying villages, on the strength of a strong value case. The approval paper records the decision but says nothing about funding, and the works will cost about £220,000. Your finance director suggests taking it from the project's £600,000 contingency reserve, since that money is already inside the programme's authorised total. How should the project manager proceed?

options.text: Ask the board to approve a budget increase or an offsetting reduction for the additional cabinets, keeping the contingency intact.
options.rationale: It funds new scope from a decision about scope, and returns the one question the approval paper left open to the body that took the decision.

options.text: Draw the £220,000 from contingency, since it is inside the authorised total and no new money is needed.
options.rationale: It funds a deliberate addition with money set aside for risks that have not happened. The programme's protection falls by a third and nothing in the reporting shows why.

options.text: Decline to start the cabinets until additional funding has been formally identified.
options.rationale: The decision has been taken by the people entitled to take it; the project manager's job is to get it funded properly, not to hold the delivery hostage to an omission in the paperwork.

options.text: Fund half from contingency and seek approval for the balance, so that the ask on the board is smaller.
options.rationale: A compromise that still misuses the reserve, and it understates the change's cost on the record, which makes the programme's real financial history unreadable later.

questions.explanation: Reserves and budget increases answer different questions: one prices what might go wrong with the agreed scope, the other funds a deliberate change to that scope. Using the first to pay for the second removes risk cover without any decision being taken about risk, and it disguises the true cost of changes in a way that compounds across a programme. Where an approval omits funding, the omission itself is the thing to escalate.
questions.mindset: New scope is funded by a decision about scope, never by the money held for risk.

questions.stem: The diagram shows how a seed-testing laboratory's project budget is built up: activity estimates roll into work packages, work packages into control accounts, control accounts into the cost baseline, with contingency inside the baseline and management reserve above it. One work package in the sample-handling control account will finish £48,000 over its estimate. Two other packages in that same control account will finish a combined £61,000 under. Select the level at which this variance should be resolved.

graphic.title: Budget build-up from activity estimates to total authorised budget
graphic.caption: Select a level of the structure. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between levels, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Work package — sample handling, robotics rig
regions.rationale: Resolving it here means treating an overspend as a problem wherever it appears, which ignores that the offsetting underspends sit inside the same account and the same manager's remit.

regions.label: Control account — sample handling
regions.rationale: This is the lowest level at which one owner holds both the overspend and the offsetting underspends, and it is the level the budget was delegated to. Managing the variance here is the account manager doing the job the structure gives them.

regions.label: Cost baseline, including contingency
regions.rationale: Reaching for contingency while the account remains within its own tolerance draws down cover the project does not need, and it teaches managers that the reserve absorbs ordinary estimating noise.

regions.label: Management reserve, above the baseline
regions.rationale: The reserve is held by the sponsor for events outside the plan. Escalating a variance that nets to a favourable position inside one account spends senior attention and suggests the delegation is not working.

questions.explanation: A budget structure exists to say who may resolve what, and a variance is handled at the lowest level whose delegated authority covers it in full. Reading only the adverse line and escalating on its size ignores the netting the structure was designed to permit; reaching past the responsible level for reserve funds converts a managed variance into a consumed contingency. What still has to happen is disclosure — the account manager reports the cause of both the overspend and the underspends, because a net position that hides two large offsetting errors is not a healthy account.
questions.mindset: Resolve a variance at the lowest level that owns every part of it.

questions.stem: A meteorological services product team of eight is funded from a standing pot rather than by quarter. Salaries and contractor rates come to £78,000 a month, and the platform charges the product carries add a further £6,000 a month. £430,000 of approved funding remains and the backlog is open-ended. Your sponsor wants to know how long the team can continue and what the next funding request should be built on.

blanks.label: Total monthly burn, in £
blanks.rationale: The people cost and the running cost are both consumed by the same team over the same month: 78,000 + 6,000 = £84,000. Excluding the platform charge is the usual error and understates the burn by more than seven per cent.

blanks.label: Complete months of runway remaining, as a whole number
blanks.rationale: 430,000 ÷ 84,000 = 5.1, so five complete months. Rounding down is deliberate: a part month of funding does not buy a part month of a team that is either engaged or not.

blanks.label: The figure the next funding request should be built on — run rate or backlog estimate
blanks.rationale: A standing team costs the same whatever is in the backlog, so cost is a function of time engaged. Building the request on a backlog estimate prices work whose scope is expected to change and produces a number that is obsolete on arrival.

questions.explanation: When a team is stable and funded continuously, money buys time rather than scope, and the forecast follows from run rate and duration. That makes the funding conversation a question of how long to keep the team, which the sponsor can answer, rather than how much the backlog will cost, which nobody can. The corollary is that runway should be reported alongside the burn, because a run rate on its own never tells anyone when a decision has to be taken.
questions.mindset: For a standing team, forecast the money from the time, and let scope be the variable.

questions.stem: Your admissions product squad at a university has a £960,000 annual envelope. The finance system reports monthly against a straight-line twelfth of that, £80,000. In month two an annual licence of £140,000 falls due as planned, and the system flags the squad as 175 per cent overspent for the month. A finance controller has asked you to explain the overrun, and the same profile will misreport three further months this year. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree a budget profile with finance that follows the expected timing of spend, so that a reported variance means something.
options.rationale: It fixes the comparator rather than the explanation. A baseline that reflects when money is genuinely due is the only version against which a variance is diagnostic.

options.text: Defer the licence renewal to a later month to smooth the reported profile.
options.rationale: It changes a real commercial decision to suit an arbitrary reporting convention, and risks a lapse in a licence the product depends on.

options.text: Explain each spike to the controller as it arises, since the annual total is correct.
options.rationale: It accepts a broken baseline and pays for it in explanations every month, and repeated false alarms train everyone to ignore the variance report altogether.

options.text: Ask for the licence cost to be reported centrally rather than against the squad.
options.rationale: Moving the cost off your report makes the variance disappear without making the forecast right, and it removes a cost the squad's own renewal decisions control.

questions.explanation: Variance is a comparison, so it is only as meaningful as the baseline profile it is measured against, and a straight-line profile imposed on lumpy spend manufactures alarms that are indistinguishable from real ones. The transferable move is to phase the budget to the expected timing of commitments before the period starts, and to treat repeated false variances as a defect in the baseline rather than a communication problem. Alarms that are routinely explained away stop being alarms.
questions.mindset: Phase the budget the way the money will actually be spent, or the variance measures the profile rather than the project.

questions.stem: You inherit a £4.1 million rural health programme delivered by nine partner organisations. What exists is a total budget, a spreadsheet of invoices received, and a sponsor who now wants a monthly forecast she can rely on. There is no structure between the total and the invoices, no named owner for any part of the budget, and no agreement about when partners report cost. Which two actions should the project manager take first?

options.text: Break the budget into control accounts, each with a named owner and an agreed scope of work.
options.rationale: Without a level between the total and the invoices, no variance can ever be attributed to anyone or anything, and a forecast becomes a guess about a single large number.

options.text: Agree with every partner how cost incurred, including work done but not yet invoiced, will be reported and by when.
options.rationale: Nine organisations invoicing on their own rhythms will produce a position that swings on billing behaviour rather than delivery, which makes month-on-month comparison meaningless.

options.text: Ask each partner for a monthly spend forecast and add them together.
options.rationale: Aggregating unvalidated figures with no agreed basis produces a total that looks authoritative and that nobody actually owns, which is worse than having no forecast.

options.text: Build a full bottom-up estimate of all remaining work before issuing any forecast.
options.rationale: It chases completeness at the cost of months in which the sponsor has nothing at all. Cost control has to start at the accuracy available now and improve.

options.text: Set a variance tolerance on the programme total and investigate only when it is breached.
options.rationale: A tolerance on a number you cannot decompose tells you something has gone wrong somewhere, at the point where it is large enough to breach, which is far too late to be useful.

questions.explanation: A cost baseline is controllable only if it has structure, ownership and an agreed reporting basis; a total with invoices underneath it has none of the three. The order matters — decomposition and ownership come before forecasting, because a forecast built on an unattributable total cannot be challenged, corrected or learned from. In multi-partner delivery the reporting basis carries as much weight as the numbers, since differing recognition practices alone can move a reported position by more than any real variance.
questions.mindset: You cannot control a number you cannot break down and hand to someone.

questions.stem: Investigation of the overspend on a solar farm grid connection programme has established three separate causes, each contributing a similar amount. Your commercial lead wants a single recovery plan, but the three causes call for different responses. Match each cause to the response that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The contractor has been supplying senior engineers where the agreed rate schedule assumed standard grades, and charging accordingly.
The same output is taking about a third more hours than estimated; the estimate's basis has been re-checked and found genuinely optimistic.
Two extra inspection surveys were requested by the client's operations team and carried out, with no change ever raised.

options.text: Challenge the charges against the rate schedule and pursue recovery commercially
options.rationale: This is a contractual question about whether what was charged matches what was agreed, so the instrument is the contract rather than the cost plan. Re-forecasting instead would concede the position without ever testing it.

options.text: Re-estimate the remaining work on observed productivity and revise the forecast
options.rationale: An estimate proved optimistic is information about all the work still to come, so the response is to re-base the forecast on what the work has actually been costing rather than to treat each month as a surprise.

options.text: Raise the additional surveys through change control and correct the baseline
options.rationale: Work the client asked for and received is added scope, and the baseline should record it. Leaving it unrecorded makes the delivery team look inefficient for doing exactly what was asked.

options.text: Increase the management reserve to cover the total overspend
options.rationale: Not used. The reserve exists for events nobody foresaw, and topping it up to cover three fully explained causes converts a diagnosis into a funding request while leaving all three causes running.

questions.explanation: Overspend is a symptom, and the response follows the cause rather than the size: a commercial breach is recovered, an estimating error is re-forecast, and unrecorded scope is brought through change control. Bundling them into one recovery plan or one funding ask loses that distinction and usually means at least two of the causes continue. The discipline that transfers is to insist on attribution before response, however uncomfortable the delay feels to whoever wants a single answer.
questions.mindset: Fix an overspend according to what caused it, not according to how large it is.

questions.stem: Engineers on your rail freight yard scheduling squad propose spending two sprints re-working a nightly batch job. It would cut the product's compute charges from about £9,400 a month to roughly £2,000. The product owner has declined, saying the roadmap is full and the sponsor funds features rather than engineering work. The engineers are frustrated and one has offered to do it quietly alongside their assigned work. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Express the proposal as an investment — two sprints of squad cost against a monthly saving — and ask the product owner to rank it on that basis.
options.rationale: It supplies the missing information rather than challenging the decision. A payback measured in a few months competes on the same terms as a feature, which is the only way it can win a place.

options.text: Let the engineer do the work quietly alongside the assigned features.
options.rationale: It hides a real investment decision and the capacity it consumes, so the squad's throughput drops for reasons the product owner cannot see and will attribute elsewhere.

options.text: Accept the product owner's ruling, since prioritisation is their call.
options.rationale: The call is theirs, but it was made without the numbers. Treating an uninformed decision as settled mistakes deference to the role for support of the person in it.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor, who is paying the compute bill and would want to know.
options.rationale: It goes around the person whose job this decision is, over a decision they have not yet had the chance to take properly, and makes the next such conversation harder.

questions.explanation: Work that reduces running cost competes with work that adds value, and it loses by default whenever it is described in engineering terms while features are described in business ones. Converting it into an investment with a payback period puts both on a comparable footing and hands the trade-off to whoever prioritises. The wider rule is that a decision-maker's judgement can only be as good as the framing they are given, and supplying a better framing is not the same as overriding them.
questions.mindset: If you want technical work prioritised, describe it in the currency the decision is made in.

questions.stem: A contractor building an access road submits an application for payment of £310,000, which includes £68,000 for drainage units described as delivered to site. Your site engineer reports that the units are on a lorry at the supplier's depot forty miles away, with delivery promised next week. The contract pays for materials only once they are on site. The contractor's commercial manager says certifying now would help their cash flow considerably. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Certify £242,000 now and set out plainly why the balance is not yet due and when it will be.
options.rationale: It pays promptly for everything properly earned while applying the condition the contract sets, and it tells the contractor exactly what has to happen for the rest to follow.

options.text: Certify the full £310,000 to support the contractor's cash position and keep the relationship constructive.
options.rationale: Paying for a condition that has not been met makes every future certificate negotiable, and it exposes the client if the units are never delivered or are diverted to another job.

options.text: Reject the application in full and ask for a corrected one next month.
options.rationale: Withholding £242,000 that is properly due punishes the whole application for one line, damages a supplier's cash for no gain, and is likely a breach of the payment terms in its own right.

options.text: Certify in full on the understanding that the amount will be recovered next month if the units have not arrived.
options.rationale: It reverses the burden. Money already paid is far harder to recover than money not yet released, and the recovery depends on remembering to do it.

questions.explanation: Certification is a statement that a defined amount of value has genuinely been earned under the contract's own rules, and it is the main control on money leaving before the client has anything to show for it. The rule that transfers is to value what has been earned and pay it promptly, while refusing what has not and explaining why — helpfulness on the timing, precision on the amount. Certifying to relieve a supplier's cash difficulty converts a payment mechanism into an unsecured loan nobody has approved.
questions.mindset: Pay quickly for what has been earned and not at all for what has not.

questions.stem: On a mining ventilation upgrade, the corporate ledger closes twelve working days after month end and the resulting cost report reaches your sponsor around five weeks after the period it covers. Decisions about labour and plant hire are therefore being taken against data that is nearly two months old, and twice this quarter a corrective action has been agreed for a problem that had already resolved itself. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Produce a timely estimated cost position from commitments, site records and supplier confirmations, reconciled to the ledger when it closes.
options.rationale: It supplies a number in time to act on and keeps it honest by reconciling later, which is the standard trade of a little precision for a great deal of relevance.

options.text: Press the finance team to close the ledger significantly faster.
options.rationale: It attacks a corporate constraint you do not control instead of the decision latency you do, and it will not change in time to help this project.

options.text: Move to quarterly cost reporting so that each report is at least complete when issued.
options.rationale: It makes the report tidier and the control weaker, tripling the period in which a cost problem can run before anyone sees it.

options.text: Continue using the ledger figure but caveat its age clearly at the top of the report.
options.rationale: Labelling data as stale does not make it usable for a decision that has to be taken now, and it transfers the problem to the reader without giving them anything better.

questions.explanation: A cost control loop is only as good as its slowest leg, and a report that arrives after the decision window has closed cannot control anything however accurate it is. The usable principle is to separate the management position, which must be timely and may be estimated, from the statutory position, which must be exact and may be late — then reconcile the two. Acting on a stale picture is how projects correct problems that have already gone away and miss the ones that have just started.
questions.mindset: A number that arrives after the decision is history, not control.

questions.stem: A new inspector joins your bridge assessment project next week, and your team lead asks you to approve about £2,000 for a laptop and survey licence from the project budget. Equipment for permanent staff normally sits on the engineering department's own budget, but this inspector is dedicated to your project for its whole duration. The cost plan you inherited does not mention staff equipment either way. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Settle with the budget holder which budget carries this class of cost, then record the answer in the cost plan.
options.rationale: It answers the question once for every similar case rather than for this laptop alone, and it turns a gap in the inherited plan into something the next person will not have to rediscover.

options.text: Approve it, since £2,000 is immaterial against the project budget.
options.rationale: Materiality is judged on the precedent as well as the amount, and a class of cost admitted without a decision accumulates quietly across a long project.

options.text: Refuse and tell the team lead to obtain the equipment from the department budget.
options.rationale: It is an answer given without checking, which is as likely to be wrong as approving would be, and it pushes the cost onto a budget holder who has not agreed to carry it.

options.text: Approve it now and reallocate the cost later if finance raises an objection.
options.rationale: Deciding first and seeking agreement afterwards turns the cost plan into a record of what happened rather than what was agreed, and reallocations after the fact rarely get done.

questions.explanation: Ambiguity about which budget carries a class of cost is cheap to resolve before the first instance and expensive afterwards, because by then a precedent exists and someone has to be told they were wrong. The general habit is to treat the first occurrence of any unclear cost as a chance to settle the rule and write it down, rather than as a one-off to be waved through on size. Small unresolved questions are the ones that recur most often.
questions.mindset: Settle the rule on the first small case, before the precedent settles it for you.

questions.stem: Your claims product squad at an insurer works to a quarterly envelope. Mid-quarter, the central platform team introduces a recharge of £30,000 a quarter for shared build and observability services, applied to every squad and backdated to the start of the quarter. You were not consulted, cannot influence the amount this period, and the charge was not in your forecast. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Re-forecast the envelope including the charge, show the sponsor what it displaces, and separately ask what drives the charge so it can be influenced next quarter.
options.rationale: It treats the current period as a fact to be reported accurately and the next period as something still open, which are two different problems that get confused when the charge feels unfair.

options.text: Dispute the charge and leave it out of the forecast until the dispute is settled.
options.rationale: A forecast that omits a cost you are actually being charged is wrong regardless of the merits of the dispute, and the sponsor discovers the gap at the worst moment.

options.text: Absorb it by leaving the vacancy on the squad unfilled for the rest of the quarter.
options.rationale: It quietly converts a cost increase into a capacity cut, which the sponsor never sees and never agreed to, and it will be read later as the team simply going slower.

options.text: Ask the platform team to waive the charge for your squad this quarter, given the notice.
options.rationale: It seeks a personal exception to a general change, solving one quarter for one squad and leaving both the structural cost and the notice problem exactly where they were.

questions.explanation: Costs allocated from elsewhere are still costs the funded work carries, and excluding them because they were unfair or unexpected produces a forecast that is precise about the parts you control and silent about the rest. The transferable split is between reporting the period you cannot change and influencing the periods you can, which usually means asking what drives the allocation rather than arguing about its existence. An allocation nobody understands is one nobody can reduce.
questions.mindset: Forecast the cost you are actually charged, and argue about the charge on its own track.

questions.stem: The sponsor of a childcare places programme tells you her monthly cost report is of no use to her. It shows the approved budget, spend to date and the percentage of budget consumed, and she says she can tell whether money has gone but not whether anything is wrong or what she should do. Which two additions would make it a document she can take decisions from?

options.text: A forecast of the final cost with the assumption it rests on stated alongside it.
options.rationale: Spend to date is history; the only figure a sponsor can act on is where the project is heading, and the assumption is what lets her judge whether to believe it.

options.text: The variance against what should have been spent for the work actually completed, with the causes of the significant items.
options.rationale: Comparing spend with progress rather than with elapsed time is what separates a project that is behind from one that is over cost, and the causes are what make the variance actionable.

options.text: A detailed breakdown of spend to date by cost type and supplier.
options.rationale: It adds detail about the past to a report whose weakness is that it says nothing about the future, and volume of detail is frequently mistaken for insight.

options.text: A monthly cash flow chart of payments made and expected.
options.rationale: A legitimate artefact aimed at the wrong reader. Cash timing is finance's question; the sponsor is asking whether the programme will land within its budget.

options.text: A red, amber or green rating for budget health on the front page.
options.rationale: A colour compresses away the judgement the sponsor is trying to make, and the rating ends up being argued over instead of the underlying numbers.

questions.explanation: A cost report earns its place by supporting a decision, which means it has to answer where the project will end up, how that compares with what was agreed, and why. Spend to date against budget answers none of these, because it compares money consumed with time elapsed and ignores what has been produced. The test for any reporting change is whether a reader could take a different action having read it — if not, the addition is decoration.
questions.mindset: Report the number someone could act on, not the number that is easiest to produce.

questions.stem: You are setting reporting conventions for a coastal ferry terminal project after finding that the previous project manager decided each case on its own merits, with the result that no two months were comparable. The two situations below have both arisen this period. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: One control account is £75,000 over while two others are under, so the project total remains within budget. This month's report should
Two work packages have finished a combined £40,000 below their estimates because those estimates were conservative. The saving should

options.text: show the control account's variance and its cause, rather than netting it off against underspends elsewhere
options.rationale: Offsetting variances have different causes and different futures, and a net position of zero conceals a problem that will keep growing while the underspends will not keep offsetting it.

options.text: be released into the project forecast so the sponsor can decide what to do with it
options.rationale: A saving that is genuine belongs to the project rather than to the manager who happened to find it, and surfacing it lets the money be redirected or returned deliberately.

options.text: be held by the account manager as informal cover against later packages overrunning
options.rationale: Not used. An undeclared buffer makes the forecast wrong by an amount only one person knows, and hidden cover is spent far more freely than cover that has been declared and argued for.

questions.explanation: Netting and hoarding are the same error viewed from two directions: both make a reported figure smoother than the reality underneath it, and both remove the information a sponsor would need to act. Reporting conventions should be set in advance so that the same situation is always treated the same way, since a rule decided case by case is decided under whatever pressure applies that month. Declared cover can be managed; undeclared cover manages you.
questions.mindset: Report the parts, because a smooth total is usually two stories cancelling each other out.

questions.stem: A developer on your fisheries licensing squad asks where she should book the two days she spent on an accessibility training course. She notes that the team books all its time to the product code because, as her colleague put it, it is simpler and the team is fully allocated to the product anyway. The squad's funding requests are built from its recorded run rate. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the time booked to what it was actually spent on, and correct the team's default so future time follows the same rule.
options.rationale: It fixes the individual case and the practice that produced it, which matters because the recorded run rate is the basis of every funding request the squad makes.

options.text: Keep booking all time to the product, since simplicity at the point of entry is worth more than precision.
options.rationale: Convenience when recording is paid for at every point of use, and it is the forecast, the capacity picture and the funding case that pay.

options.text: Book the training to the product, since the skills gained will be applied to the product.
options.rationale: A plausible-sounding rule that makes the run rate unusable for planning capacity, because the number then mixes days spent building with days spent not building.

options.text: Leave it and ask finance to make an adjustment at year end.
options.rationale: It defers the correction to a point where nobody remembers the facts, and the reports issued in the meantime — including the funding request — stay wrong.

questions.explanation: Time records are the raw material of cost actuals in people-heavy delivery, and every distortion introduced at entry propagates into the run rate, the forecast and the funding conversation. Booking effort to what it was actually spent on is what keeps capacity and cost separable — a team of eight funded for eight is not a team of eight delivering for eight. Defaults set for convenience are worth revisiting precisely because nobody notices them.
questions.mindset: Record effort against what it was spent on, because everything downstream inherits the answer.

questions.stem: Your organisation has imposed a ten per cent in-year reduction on every project, and the programme office has asked each manager to return a revised budget by Friday with the money removed. Your £3.6 million programme has one workstream driven by a regulatory deadline that cannot move, and two discretionary improvement workstreams delivered iteratively. The reduction is not negotiable in total. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Return a re-planned budget that takes the reduction where it forfeits least value, stating explicitly what will not now be delivered.
options.rationale: It accepts the constraint and spends the only discretion available — where the cut lands — while making the consequence visible to whoever imposed it.

options.text: Reduce every workstream by ten per cent so the burden is shared evenly.
options.rationale: An even cut looks fair and is not: it protects the appearance of neutrality by putting a regulatory commitment at risk alongside optional improvements.

options.text: Take the whole reduction from contingency, leaving the delivery plan untouched.
options.rationale: It preserves the plan by removing the cover for its risks, so the cut resurfaces later as an overrun and the organisation never sees the real trade-off it made.

options.text: Decline to submit until the regulatory workstream has been formally exempted.
options.rationale: Refusing to engage with a portfolio decision forfeits the chance to shape where the cut falls, and someone less informed will make the allocation instead.

questions.explanation: An imposed reduction removes the choice about how much but leaves the choice about what, and that second choice is where a project manager adds value. Uniform trimming and contingency raids are both ways of avoiding the prioritisation conversation, and both are paid for later — in commitments missed or risks uncovered. Stating what the reduction forfeits is also what allows the decision to be revisited if the consequence turns out to be unacceptable.
questions.mindset: When the amount is fixed, the judgement is about what you give up — so make that visible.

questions.stem: A film archive digitisation package has been estimated three ways by the team that will do the work: £180,000 if the reels are in the condition the sample suggested, £220,000 on the most likely condition, and £320,000 if around a third of them need chemical treatment before scanning. Your finance partner wants one figure for the cost plan and a defensible basis for whatever contingency you intend to ask for.

blanks.label: Expected cost using the weighted three-point formula, in £
blanks.rationale: Weighting the most likely case four times gives (180,000 + 880,000 + 320,000) ÷ 6 = £230,000. The long tail on the pessimistic side pulls the expected value above the most likely value, which is the whole point of the calculation.

blanks.label: Standard deviation of the estimate, in £
blanks.rationale: The spread is (320,000 − 180,000) ÷ 6 = £23,333. It gives the range a size, which is what turns a contingency request into an argument rather than a preference.

blanks.label: What the £10,000 difference between the most likely figure and the expected figure should be held as
blanks.rationale: It is the amount by which the asymmetry of the estimate exceeds the most likely case, so it is cover for a known uncertainty rather than an increase in the base cost — which is exactly what contingency inside the baseline is for.

questions.explanation: A three-point estimate produces two useful outputs: a central figure that accounts for the shape of the uncertainty, and a spread that sizes it. Publishing the most likely value as the plan commits the project to the best of the three cases and leaves the tail unfunded, which is how projects arrive at overspends that were foreseeable from the first estimate. The spread also tells you where refinement is worth buying — a wide range on a large package is worth investigating before it is priced.
questions.mindset: Plan on the figure that accounts for the tail, and say plainly what the difference from the optimistic case is for.

questions.stem: Two squads at a bicycle hire operator share a single £600,000 half-year budget line. The maintenance app squad is tracking under its planned spend, and the rider app squad wants £45,000 moved across now to bring in a contractor for the rest of the period. Both product owners are content and the line's total would not change. Which two actions should the project manager take before any money moves?

options.text: Confirm who holds the authority to move funds within that line and what the move must be recorded against.
options.rationale: A budget line is an authorisation with conditions attached, not a pot two willing parties may rearrange, and the conditions usually specify who may vary it and how.

options.text: Re-forecast both squads to the end of the period before agreeing the transfer.
options.rationale: An underspend that is late recruitment rather than a genuine saving evaporates when the hire lands, and moving it would leave the first squad short in the last weeks of the period.

options.text: Move the money, since the total on the line is unchanged and both product owners agree.
options.rationale: It treats agreement between the two spenders as sufficient authority, which is precisely the check a shared budget line exists to impose.

options.text: Refuse until the next scheduled funding review so the change can be considered properly.
options.rationale: It turns an ordinary in-period decision into a wait that costs delivery, when what is needed is the right approval rather than a different meeting.

options.text: Transfer half the amount now as a compromise and review the rest later.
options.rationale: Splitting the difference answers neither the authority question nor the forecast question, and leaves the rider squad with a contractor engagement it cannot fully fund.

questions.explanation: Money moving inside a total looks like a neutral act and is not: it changes what each part of the work has been authorised to spend, and it usually rests on an underspend nobody has tested. The two checks that transfer are authority — who may vary this, and on what record — and reality, meaning whether the surplus is a saving or merely a timing difference. Both are quick, and skipping them is how organisations discover at period end that the same money was counted twice.
questions.mindset: An underspend is not money until you have checked it is not just late.

questions.stem: Your £8.4 million harbour operations programme reports total cost incurred against its baseline. The corporate finance system splits the same spend between capital and revenue under recognition rules that defer some costs and expense others immediately. For the same period, finance reports £6.1 million to the board and your programme report shows £6.9 million. Both figures are correct on their own basis. The audit committee has asked which one is right. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Publish a single reconciled position that shows both bases, itemises what causes the difference, and states which basis governs programme decisions.
options.rationale: It stops the two figures competing by making the bridge between them part of the reporting, and it settles in advance which number is used for which purpose.

options.text: Adopt the finance figure as the single source of truth for all programme reporting.
options.rationale: A basis built for statutory recognition defers and reclassifies costs for reasons unrelated to delivery, so managing against it loses the timing information that cost control depends on.

options.text: Explain the difference verbally at the committee and continue with both reports as they are.
options.rationale: A difference that has to be re-explained each period will be re-litigated each period, and the explanation is only as durable as the memory of whoever heard it.

options.text: Ask finance to change its treatment of the programme's costs so the two reports agree.
options.rationale: It asks a statutory process to bend to a management report, which it cannot do, and spends the programme's credibility on a request that will be refused.

questions.explanation: Two correct numbers for the same thing are not a contradiction to be resolved by picking one, but a difference in basis to be documented and bridged. The general rule is that management reporting and statutory reporting answer different questions and should be allowed to differ, provided the reconciliation is published and the governing basis for decisions is agreed. Unexplained divergence between two authoritative figures is corrosive: it invites every party to quote whichever supports their position.
questions.mindset: When two right answers disagree, publish the bridge rather than choosing a side.

questions.stem: A control account manager on a distillery bottling line project tells you privately that his account looks likely to overrun by around £90,000, because of a change in the way his supplier is charging for stainless steel fabrication. He asks you to leave it out of this month's report while he confirms the cause with the supplier, arguing that reporting a figure he cannot yet substantiate would be irresponsible. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Report the forecast movement now with its uncertainty stated and the investigation noted as under way.
options.rationale: A forecast is allowed to carry uncertainty, and saying so is what distinguishes an early warning from a claim. The sponsor gets a month of options that silence would have cost.

options.text: Agree to wait a month, since reporting an unconfirmed number could turn out to be wrong.
options.rationale: It sets a standard of certainty that forecasts can never meet, so every genuine early warning would be suppressed until it was too late to be worth having.

options.text: Report the £90,000 as a firm forecast variance without qualification.
options.rationale: It overstates confidence in a number still being investigated, and when the figure moves it costs credibility that the next warning will need.

options.text: Record it on the risk register instead, until the cause is confirmed.
options.rationale: Something already happening is an issue rather than a risk, and filing it as a risk delays the response while making the register a place where inconvenient facts are parked.

questions.explanation: Forecasts are estimates and their value lies in lead time, so requiring certainty before reporting destroys most of what makes them useful.
