The reportable unit is a range with its basis and confidence attached, not a single confirmed number, and stating the uncertainty explicitly is what allows figures to move later without anyone's credibility moving with them. A culture that punishes revised forecasts reliably produces late ones.
questions.mindset: Report the movement with its uncertainty attached rather than waiting for a number you can defend absolutely.

questions.stem: At a quarterly review for a wildlife monitoring product, your sponsor asks three questions in quick succession and your finance analyst starts answering all of them with the same figure. Each question is actually asking about a different thing. Match each question to the figure that answers it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: How much of this quarter's funding has actually left the organisation so far?
What have we already tied ourselves to for next quarter, whether or not anyone has billed us yet?
If the squad carries on exactly as it is, what will the rest of the year cost?

options.text: Spend to date
options.rationale: This is the only one of the figures that describes money that has genuinely gone, which is precisely what the question asks and nothing more.

options.text: Committed cost not yet invoiced
options.rationale: Signed engagements and orders consume future funding before any invoice appears, so this is what tells a sponsor how much of the next period is already spoken for.

options.text: Forecast cost, run rate multiplied by the months remaining
options.rationale: A continuation question is a forecast question, and for a standing team the honest projection is the current run rate extended across the time remaining.

options.text: The approved funding envelope
options.rationale: Not used. The envelope is what was authorised, which none of the three questions asked about, and offering it in answer to any of them substitutes permission to spend for information about spending.

questions.explanation: Money questions look interchangeable and are not: what has gone, what is already promised, and what is still to come are three different figures that move independently and can each be right while the others look wrong. Answering with the wrong one is the most common way a cost conversation goes astray, because the sponsor accepts the number and reaches a conclusion the number does not support. Naming which figure you are quoting costs a sentence and prevents most of that.
questions.mindset: Say which figure you are quoting, because spent, committed and forecast are three different answers.

questions.stem: At month nine your schools kitchen refurbishment programme shows £420,000 under budget. The cause is a subcontract that was due to start in month seven and will now start in month eleven; the work and its cost are unchanged. The portfolio office has seen the position and proposes reallocating £300,000 of it to another programme that is short this year. Your sponsor asks for your view before the portfolio board meets. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Show the re-profiled forecast demonstrating the underspend is timing rather than saving, and let the reallocation be decided against that.
options.rationale: It converts a misleading snapshot into the shape of the spend, so a decision to reallocate, if taken, is taken knowing the bill still arrives.

options.text: Agree to release the £300,000, since it demonstrably will not be spent in this financial year.
options.rationale: It confuses a phasing difference with money the programme does not need. The subcontract still has to be paid, and it will arrive with no budget behind it.

options.text: Refuse on the basis that the money is committed to the subcontract.
options.rationale: A flat refusal without the profile gives the portfolio office nothing to decide on, and committed is not the same as contracted — the distinction will be tested.

options.text: Offer the full £420,000, since cooperation now will make future funding requests easier.
options.rationale: It buys goodwill with money the programme will need, and the goodwill will not be available at the point the shortfall appears.

questions.explanation: An underspend has to be diagnosed before it can be treated, because a saving and a delay look identical in a cumulative figure and have opposite implications. The transferable response is to answer with the profile rather than with a yes or a no: showing when the money is now needed lets a legitimate portfolio decision be taken on real information. Where the deferred cost crosses a funding boundary, that consequence belongs in the same conversation rather than in next year's.
questions.mindset: Ask whether an underspend is a saving or a delay before anyone spends it.

questions.stem: Two of the nine people on your livestock traceability squad left mid-quarter and were backfilled two weeks later by contractors at noticeably higher day rates. Six weeks on, a finance analyst asks why the squad's cost has not fallen and whether the forecast should be reduced to reflect the smaller team she was told about. The envelope for the quarter has not changed. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Re-forecast from the squad's actual composition and rates, and explain that cost moved with rate and timing rather than with headcount.
options.rationale: It answers the question with a revised number and repairs the assumption behind it, which is what stops the same query arriving next quarter.

options.text: Reduce the forecast by two ninths for the period the two roles were vacant.
options.rationale: A proportional adjustment treats people as interchangeable units of cost and ignores both the two-week gap and the higher contractor rates that followed it.

options.text: Leave the forecast unchanged, since the quarter's envelope has not moved.
options.rationale: It confuses the authorised limit with the expected cost. An envelope says what may be spent; a forecast says what will be, and only the second answers her question.

options.text: Attribute the difference to contractor rates and leave the numbers as they are.
options.rationale: Naming a cause without producing a revised figure leaves the analyst with an explanation and no number, so the forecast in the system stays wrong.

questions.explanation: For a people-funded team, cost is driven by who is engaged, at what rate, for how long — so headcount alone predicts very little. Any change of composition should trigger a re-forecast rather than a proportional adjustment, because vacancies, notice periods and rate differences rarely align with the arithmetic anyone assumes. Answering a challenge to a forecast with a revised forecast, rather than with a justification, is also what keeps the number in the system trustworthy.
questions.mindset: When a team changes, re-forecast from who is actually engaged and at what rate.

questions.stem: Your £6.8 million airport stand refurbishment is in its final quarter and forecasts a £300,000 underspend, almost all of it undrawn contingency. The finance director wants it released now to fund another scheme that is short before year end. Commissioning and a load test remain, and three high-impact risks on the register are still open until the stands are handed over. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Re-price the exposure that remains open and recommend releasing only the amount that exceeds it.
options.rationale: Reserve adequacy is a function of what is still to come, and the remaining tests are exactly where the identified risks would materialise. Partial release is usually available and is the honest answer.

options.text: Put the release decision, together with what it would mean if the open risks occur, to whoever authorised the reserve.
options.rationale: The reserve was established by a decision and can only be reduced by one, and the person who took it should see the exposure they would be accepting on the project's behalf.

options.text: Release the full £300,000 now and raise a change request later if one of the risks occurs.
options.rationale: It assumes money can be recalled at the moment of need, which is precisely when other commitments have absorbed it and the request is hardest to argue.

options.text: Refuse any release until practical completion, when the risks are certain to have passed.
options.rationale: Holding cover beyond the exposure that justifies it starves the portfolio of money that could be working, and it is the mirror image of the error in releasing too much.

options.text: Transfer the contingency to the other scheme's budget while retaining a claim on it should it be needed.
options.rationale: A claim on money sitting in someone else's budget is not cover: it depends on their spending pattern and their willingness, neither of which the project controls.

questions.explanation: Releasing reserve early and holding it too long are both failures, and the discipline that resolves them is the same: value the remaining exposure and hold cover proportionate to it, revisiting as risks close. Reserves belong to whoever authorised them, so the project manager's role is to supply the exposure analysis rather than to make the release decision or to resist it on principle. A reserve released with an informal promise of return has been spent, whatever the arrangement is called.
questions.mindset: Hold reserve against the exposure that is left, and give back the rest deliberately.

questions.stem: A shared parcel locker product squad is funded jointly, sixty per cent by the retail division and forty per cent by logistics. Retail's director tells you his division must cut costs and will reduce his contribution by a third from next month. Logistics is unwilling to make up the difference. The squad is halfway through a fulfilment feature that both divisions need, and neither director has spoken to the other about it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Translate the reduction into its effect on capacity and on the shared roadmap, and take that to both funders as one decision.
options.rationale: It reframes a unilateral budget cut as a joint decision about shared work, which is what it actually is, and puts the two people who must resolve it in the same conversation.

options.text: Reduce the squad by the equivalent of retail's cut and continue with the remaining capacity.
options.rationale: It assumes the work divides cleanly by funder when both divisions need the same feature, so logistics silently loses delivery it is still paying full price for.

options.text: Ask logistics to cover the shortfall temporarily until retail's position improves.
options.rationale: It shifts the burden without addressing the cause, and an informal subsidy becomes a claim on priority and ownership that will surface at the worst possible moment.

options.text: Continue at full capacity and report the overspend when it appears in the quarter's figures.
options.rationale: It spends money that has not been authorised in the hope that the funders resolve it in the meantime, which leaves the project manager holding a decision that was never theirs.

questions.explanation: Where several funders buy shared capacity, a change by any one of them is a change to what everyone receives, and treating it as a private matter between one funder and the team produces silent losses for the others. The move that transfers is to convert money into its delivery consequence and put that single picture in front of all the funders together, because only they can decide between less capacity, a different split and a narrower roadmap. Shared funding needs a shared forum, and its absence is usually the real problem.
questions.mindset: When funding is shared, a change by one funder is a decision for all of them.
